**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Geology 2 (0755), Paper 2, ADVANCED LEVEL, JUNE 2026. Duration: THREE HOURS.**

Instructions to candidates: Answer FOUR questions. ALL QUESTIONS CARRY EQUAL MARKS.

Question 3(c) : le total des elements de symetrie est donne pour les systemes cubique (23), tetragonal (11), orthorhombique (7), hexagonal (15) et monoclinique (3) d'apres la symetrie de la classe holoedrique ; pour le systeme trigonal, seuls les elements sont listes (certains manuels le rattachent au systeme hexagonal, d'ou 6 ou 7 systemes). questions.enonce_markdown:
(a) Explain how bonding in minerals influences their physical properties.

(6 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
The **type of chemical bond** between the atoms or ions of a mineral, and the strength and arrangement of these bonds in its structure, determine its **hardness, cleavage, melting point, solubility, electrical conductivity, lustre and density**. Strong bonds in all directions give hard, high-melting minerals; a weak bond in one direction gives a soft mineral with cleavage in that direction.

| Type of bond | Nature | Effect on physical properties | Examples |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Ionic** | Electrostatic attraction between positive and negative ions in a regular lattice | Moderate hardness, **brittle**, fairly high melting point; **cleavage** along planes of ions; **soluble in water**; poor conductors as solids but conduct when molten or dissolved; glassy (vitreous) lustre | Halite (NaCl), fluorite, calcite |
| **Covalent** | Atoms share electrons in a strong, directional 3-D network | **Very hard**, very high melting point, **insoluble**, **electrical insulators**, brilliant (adamantine) lustre | Diamond, quartz (Si-O bonds, partly covalent), corundum |
| **Metallic** | Positive ions in a "sea" of free electrons | **Malleable and ductile** (not brittle), **good conductors of heat and electricity**, **metallic lustre**, opaque, usually high density | Native gold, silver, copper |
| **Van der Waals (weak residual bonds)** | Weak electrical attraction between layers or molecules | **Very soft**, **perfect cleavage** parallel to the weak layers, low melting point, greasy or pearly feel, light | Graphite (between its layers), talc, sulphur |
| **Hydrogen bonds** | Attraction involving H in water or OH groups | Weak bonding, soft, low melting point; perfect cleavage in sheets | Ice, gypsum (water layers), clay minerals |

**Mixed bonding.** Many minerals have more than one type of bond, and the **weakest bond controls the cleavage**: in **graphite**, carbon atoms in sheets are bonded covalently (strong) while the sheets are held by Van der Waals bonds, so graphite is soft, slippery and has perfect cleavage and conducts electricity, while **diamond**, which has the same chemical composition (C) but bonding in all three directions, is the hardest mineral. In **mica** the silicate sheets are strongly bonded but are joined by weak ionic bonds of K, so mica has **perfect basal cleavage** and is soft.

**Other effects.** Bond strength and length (together with the radius and charge of the ions) also control **density** (packed structures with heavy atoms are denser), **fracture** (conchoidal in minerals without cleavage and with strong bonds in all directions, as in quartz) and **refractive index and lustre**.

**(i) Crystal zone and crystal axis (3 marks)**

| Crystal zone | Crystal axis |
|---|---|
| A **set of crystal faces whose edges of intersection are all parallel** to one direction (a line called the **zone axis**). For example, the prism faces of a quartz crystal form a zone whose zone axis is parallel to the c axis. | An **imaginary reference line passing through the centre of the crystal**, used to describe the position of the faces of the crystal; there are three (a, b, c) in most systems (four in the hexagonal system). |
| Describes a **group of faces** (a relationship between faces). | Describes a **direction**, a reference in space for the **whole crystal**. |
| Its axis is a direction of the edges and **need not be a crystallographic axis**. | Is fixed by the crystal system and its length ratio. |

**(ii) Parameters of a crystal and Miller indices (3 marks)**

| Parameters | Miller indices |
|---|---|
| The **distances (intercepts) cut off by a crystal face on the crystallographic axes**, measured in units of the axial lengths a, b and c of the standard (unit) face; for example a face cutting the axes at 2a, 3b, 6c has parameters 2 : 3 : 6 (**Weiss parameters**). | The **reciprocals of the parameters, cleared of fractions** (multiplied by the lowest common multiple) and written in brackets without commas, (hkl). |
| Shows where the face meets the axes; a face parallel to an axis has an intercept of **infinity**. | A face parallel to an axis has the index **0**, so it is easier to use than infinity. |

Example: parameters 2 : 3 : 6 give reciprocals 1/2 : 1/3 : 1/6, which are multiplied by 6 to give the Miller indices **(3 2 1)**. The unit face (1 : 1 : 1) has the indices (1 1 1); a face parallel to the b and c axes and cutting a at 1 has parameters 1 : infinity : infinity, so the indices are (1 0 0).

**(iii) Crystallographic axis and axis of symmetry (3 marks)**

| Crystallographic axis | Axis of symmetry |
|---|---|
| An **imaginary reference line** (a, b, c) used to describe the position of the faces and to define the **crystal system** (by the lengths and the angles between the axes). | An **imaginary line through the crystal about which the crystal can be rotated through 360° so that it presents the same appearance 2, 3, 4 or 6 times** (a diad, triad, tetrad or hexad axis). |
| Is a **reference** for description; every crystal has three (or four) of them. | Is a **symmetry element**; a crystal may have several, one or none (triclinic crystals have none, except the centre of symmetry). |
| Fixed by the lengths and angles of the unit cell, and **may or may not** coincide with an axis of symmetry. | Is fixed by the **symmetry** of the crystal; in the cubic system the three crystallographic axes coincide with the tetrad axes, and in the orthorhombic system with the three diads. |

questions.enonce_markdown:
(c) Classify crystals into crystal systems based on the diagnostic symmetry elements of the respective holosymmetric classes.

(10 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Crystals are placed in **seven crystal systems** (some books combine the trigonal system with the hexagonal system to give six), according to the lengths of the crystallographic axes, the angles between them and, above all, the **diagnostic symmetry elements**. The **holosymmetric class** (the class with the highest symmetry, the one with the most symmetry elements) is the typical class of each system. The classification is as follows.

| System | Axes and angles | Holosymmetric class and its symmetry elements | Diagnostic element | Examples |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Cubic (isometric)** | a = b = c; all angles 90° | Hexoctahedral class: **3 tetrad axes, 4 triad axes, 6 diad axes, 9 planes, a centre of symmetry (23 elements in all)** | **Four triad (3-fold) axes** | Halite, galena, fluorite, pyrite, garnet |
| **Tetragonal** | a = b ≠ c; all angles 90° | Ditetragonal dipyramidal class: **1 tetrad axis (c), 4 diad axes, 5 planes, a centre (11 elements)** | **One tetrad (4-fold) axis** | Zircon, rutile, cassiterite |
| **Orthorhombic** | a ≠ b ≠ c; all angles 90° | Rhombic dipyramidal class: **3 diad axes (along a, b, c), 3 planes, a centre (7 elements)** | **Three mutually perpendicular diads (or planes)** | Olivine, barite, topaz, sulphur |
| **Hexagonal** | a1 = a2 = a3 ≠ c; the three a axes at 120° in one plane and c at 90° to them | Dihexagonal dipyramidal class: **1 hexad axis (c), 6 diad axes, 7 planes, a centre (15 elements)** | **One hexad (6-fold) axis** | Beryl, apatite |
| **Trigonal (rhombohedral)** | Same axes as hexagonal (or three equal axes at equal angles not 90°) | Ditrigonal scalenohedral class: **1 triad (3-fold) axis, 3 diad axes, 3 planes, a centre** | **One triad axis** (with no tetrad or hexad) | Calcite, dolomite, quartz, corundum |
| **Monoclinic** | a ≠ b ≠ c; alpha = gamma = 90°, beta ≠ 90° | Prismatic class: **1 diad axis (b), 1 plane perpendicular to it, a centre (3 elements)** | **One diad axis (or one plane)** | Gypsum, orthoclase, mica, augite, hornblende |
| **Triclinic** | a ≠ b ≠ c; no angle is 90° | Pinacoidal class: **only a centre of symmetry** (no axes, no planes) | **No axis or plane; only a centre of symmetry** | Albite and other plagioclase feldspars, kyanite, microcline |

**To place a crystal:** first look for **triads**: four of them means cubic; one with no 4-fold or 6-fold axis means trigonal. A **hexad** means hexagonal, a **tetrad** means tetragonal. If only **diads** or planes are present, three perpendicular diads give orthorhombic, a single diad gives monoclinic, and none gives triclinic.

*Marking idea: each system with its axial relation, its diagnostic element and an example (about 1.5 marks per system, 10 in all).*
